The Great AI Chip Heist Is Here

Up to a third of China’s compute may come from chips smuggled through a booming black market.

By

Greg Lui thought frogs were his ticket to riches. So in 2012, according to public profiles, he co-founded a Chinese restaurant in Arcadia, Calif., serving frogs and other savory delights in fiery Sichuan sauces. When diners proved less than enthusiastic, he cooked up another business project, a technology company, which culminated in his arrest last month. He is charged with smuggling more than $300 million worth of high-end graphics processing unit servers to China through Malaysia. Mr. Lui hasn’t entered a plea.

The widespread smuggling of high-end AI chips may be the worst case of technology theft in history in financial volume and national-security risk. According to the research institute Epoch AI, between 290,000 and 1.6 million Nvidia H100-equivalent chips had been smuggled into China by the end of 2025, forming potentially a third of China’s current total computing capacity.
